doc.title: Warren Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 17, 2018

title: Playing in Harry Partch's ensemble and the bass marimba
summary: Smith performed in Partch's ensemble in his last year of college, played the four-note bass marimba and drove Partch's truck home.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: The year that I left college, in 1957, Harry Partch came to the college and did a residency. And I performed in his ensemble and rehearsed with him for the whole year, and then when that event was finished we put all his stuff in a truck and I drove his truck back up to Ohio, in Yellow Springs or someplace, Ohio, and then brought the memories and the truck back with me. That was probably the first really outstanding experience.
What was your role in that?

I played an instrument called the bass marimba. It was, his octave was not a tempered 12- key octave. His octave had about 43 tones in it. So he had a lot of microtones. But he had built all these instruments himself, and one I remember was a bass marimba. It had four notes. And you had to play it with the handle, with a mallet, the handle was the size of the lower end of a baseball bat, and the ball that hit the instrument was bigger than, it was about the size of a sixteen inch softball. But it was made out of fiber, or some kind — and you hit it, and this one big note, you couldn’t hear it at all. It had sixteen vibrations and you could see it vibrating. You couldn’t hear it but you could feel the vibrations in your stomach. And there were a lot of things about Harry Partch that I’ll never forget you know, but the way that he composed his music and rehearsed us and whatnot was just, that was probably the first real professional challenge in my life, even before I got into the profession, where I was making a living at it.
Did you, at that time, start to think that’s one of the things I would like to do. What he’s doing? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
